  Kl. W., Kluge, Wörterbuch.

  Kuhns zs., Zeitschrift für vergleichende sprachforschung. Berlin
      1852 ff.

  Litbl., Literaturblatt für germ. und roman. philologie. Heilbronn
      1880 ff.

  Sk., Skeat, Etymological Dictionary.

  vB., von Bahder, Verbalabstracta.

  Wrede, Wand., Sprache der Wandalen, s. § 220 n. 4.

  Wrede, Ostg., Sprache der Ostgoten, s. § 221 n. 4.

  Zs. fda., Zeitschrift für deutsches alterthum. Berlin 1841 ff. With
      this sinse vol. 19: Anzeiger für d. alt. Berlin 1876 ff.

  Zs. fdph., Zeitschrift für deutsche philologie. Halle 1869 ff.




FONOLOGY.




CHAP. I. THE ALFABET.


§ 1. The monuments of the Gothic language ar handed down to us in a
peculiar alfabet which, according to Greek ecclesiastic writers, was
invented by Wulfila (s. § 221). The Gothic alfabet, however, is not
entirely a new creation, but Wulfila based it on the Greek alfabet
which he accomodated to the Gothic sounds, increasing it by several
signs from the Latin alfabet, and, in a few cases, availing himself
of the familiar runic alfabet. Of the Greek alfabet he also retaind
the order and numerical value. The Gothic alfabet is now sufficiently
represented in Roman letters. In the following we giv in the first line
the original Gothic characters, in the second their numerical values,
in the third the transliteration of the Gothic characters by Roman
letters, which latter we shall uze exclusivly in this book.

[Illustration:

   A    B    Γ    d    e    u    z    h    Ψ

   1    2    3    4    5    6    7    8    9

   a    b    g    d    e    q    z    h    þ

   ϊι   R    λ    M    N    G    n    Π    ɥ

   10   20   30   40   50   60   70   80   90

   i    k    l    m    n    j    u    p    --

   R    S    T    Y    Ꝼ    X    Θ    Ω    ↑

  100  200  300  400  500  600  700  800  900

   r    s    t    w    f    χ    ƕ    o    --]

  NOTE 1. Of these signs one (=i=, _10_) is represented by two forms.
  The =i= without dots occurs oftener, the =i= with dots stands at
  the beginning of a word, and in the midl of a word after a vowel,
  to show that it forms a syllabl for itself and does not form a
  difthong with the preceding vowel; e. g., =fraïtiþ= (= =fra-itiþ=).
  In transliteration =i= is employd thruout.

  NOTE 2. Two characters, the Greek episema 'koppa' (_90_) and
  'sampi' (_900_), hav no fonetic values, but serv only as numerals.
  When the symbols denote numerals, they ar markt by a horizontal
  stroke abuv them, or by dots before and after them: =i̅b̅= or
  =·ib·= = 12.

  NOTE 3. The transliteration of the Gothic symbols is not alike in
  all cases. Most editors hav hitherto uzed =v= for =w= (§ 39, n. 1);
  for the singl symbols =q= (§ 39, n. 1) and =ƕ= (§ 63) we find =kv=
  or =qu= and =hv= or =w=, respectivly; for =þ=, which is borrowd
  from the Norse-A.-S. alfabet, also =th= occurs (§ 70, n. 1).

  NOTE 4. The Gothic monuments show but few abbreviations; the holy
  names, =guþ=, =frauja=, =iêsus=, =Χristus=, ar always abbreviated.
  Abbreviations ar denoted by a stroke abuv the word, but in our
  texts the abbreviated words ar uzually printed in ful; as, =g̅þ̅= =
  =guþ=, =f̅a̅=, =f̅i̅n̅s̅= = =frauja=, =fraujins=.--For more on this
  point, s. Gabelentz-Loebe's grammar, p. 19 et seq.

  NOTE 5. The Goths alredy had the Germanic runic letters before
  Wulfila. The names of these letters wer uzed also for the new
  characters. The names of the Gothic symbols, together with a
  few Gothic words and alfabets, ar preservd in a Salzburg-Vienna
  manuscript of the 9th century: W. Grimm, 'Wiener Jahrbücher der
  Litteratur 43', p. 4 et seq. Massmann, zs. fda. 1, p. 296 et
  seq.--The form of the names, however, is very corrupt. As to
  this, cp. A. Kirchhoff, 'Das Gotische Runenalphabet', 2nd edit.,
  Berlin 1854; J. Zacher, 'Das Gotische Alphabet Vulfilas und das
  Runenalphabet', Leipzig 1855.--Of special importance is Wimmer's
  treatis on Wulfila's alfabet, as 'Appendix I' to his book: 'Die
  Runenschrift', Berlin 1887, pp. 259-274.

§ 2. Of the 27 characters two hav only numerical values, (§ 1, n. 2), a
third, the χ, is retaind only in Greek foren words, especially in the
name 'Christus', and denotes no Gothic sound. Hense there remain the
following 24 characters whose fonetic values ar to be determind:

(a) Consonants:

  =p b f m w | t d þ s z n l r | k q g h ƕ j.=

(b) Vowels:

  =a e i o u.=

(c) Difthongs:

  =ei iu ai au.=

In determining the fonetic values of these characters we ar guided
by the following means: (1) The Gothic alfabet is based on the Greek
alfabet; hense, the pronunciation of the Greek letters to be determind
for the 4th century, must also be regarded as that of the Gothic
letters so long as there is no proof to the contrary. (2) The rendition
of the numerous Greek foren words and proper nouns by Wulfila. (3)
The transliteration of the Gothic proper nouns in Latin documents
and by Latin authors of the 4th-8th centuries. (4) The testimony of
the cognate Germanic languages. (5) Fonetic changes and grammatical
fenomena in the Gothic language itself permit us to draw conclusions
about the nature of the sounds.

  NOTE 1. Concerning the pronunciation of the Gothic letters, cp.
  Weingärtner, 'Die Aussprache des Gotischen zur Zeit des Ulfilas',
  Leipzig 1858; Fr. Dietrich, 'Ueber die Aussprache des Gotischen
  während der Zeit seines Bestehens', Marburg 1862; about the
  consonants, Paul, 'Zur Lautverschiebung', Beitr. 1, p. 147 et seq.

  NOTE 2. An old testimony for the Gothic pronunciation in the
  Salzburg-Vienna MS.:

  _uuortun  otan   auar  euangeliū   ther   lucam_
  =waurþun  uþþan  afar  aiwaggeljo  þairh  Lokan=

      _uuorthun  auar  thuo  iachuedant iachᵘatun_
      =waurþun   afar  þo    jah qeþun.=

  ubi dicit. genuit _.j._ ponitur     ubi gabriel _.g._ ponunt et
  alia his sim̅ ubi aspiratione . ut dicitur gah libeda _jah libaida_
      diptongon _ai_ pro e longa    p ch _q_ ponunt.--Cp. § 1, n. 5,
  and, for explanation, especially Kirchhoff, p. 20 et seq.




CHAP. II. THE VOWELS.


a

§ 3. The Gothic =a= signifies as a rule the short a-sound [as in G.
mann].

  NOTE 1. Foren words and names; as, =Annas=, Ἀννας; =Akaja=, Ἀχαΐα;
  =barbarus=, βάρβαρος; =aggilus=, ἄγγελος; =karkara=, _carcer_;
  =lukarn=, _lucerna_; =Kafarnaum=, Καπερναούμ.

  NOTE 2. Gothic names: =Athanaricus=, =Ariaricus=, =Amalafrigda=
  (_Ammian._)

§ 4. Short =a= is very frequent both in stem-syllabls and in
inflection. E. g.

(a) Stem-syllabls: =agis=, _aw_; =aljis=, '_alius_'; =tagr=, _tear_;
=aƕa=, '_aqua_'; =alan=, _to grow_; =hafjan=, _to heav_; =saltan=, _to
salt_; =haldan=, _to hold_; =waldan=, _to rule_; =fadar=, _father_;
=staþs=, _place_.--=ahtau=, '_octo_'; =gasts=, _guest_; =ƕaþar=,
'_uter_'; =awistr=, _sheepfold_ (OHG. au, '_ovis_'; ahd. gr., § 219, n.
3); =bandi=, _band_; =barn=, _child_; =saggws=, _song_; all preterits
of the III.-V. ablaut-series: =bar=, _I bore_; =hlaf=, _I stole_;
=band=, _I bound_; =gaf=, _I gave_, etc.

(b) Inflections: =daga= (dat. sg., § 90), =waúrda= (nom. acc. pl., §
93), =giba= (nom. acc. sg., § 96), =guma= (nom. sg., § 107), =haírtôna=
(nom. acc. pl., § 109); --=blindamma=, =blindana=, =blinda=, =blindata=
(str. adj., § 123); --=imma=, =ina=, =ita=, =ija=, =meina= (prn.; § 150
et seq.); --=nima= (1st pers. sg. prs. ind.); =nimaima=, =nimaiwa=,
=nimaina= (1st pers. pl. du. and 3d pers. pl. opt., § 170); =haitada=
(medio-passiv, § 170); =sôkida= (weak prt., § 184); --adverbs: =-ba=
(as, =glaggwuba=), =nêƕa=, =inna=, =ana=, =waíla=, etc.

  NOTE 1. Apocope of an unaccented =a= before enclitics:
  =þat-ist=, =þat-ei=, =þan-uh=, =þamm-uh=, =þan-ei=, =þamm-ei=,
  =kar-ist=.--Also =frêt= and =frêtum= (prt. of =fra-itan=, _to
  devour_, § 176, n. 3).

  NOTE 2. For =a= in the difthongs =ai=, =au=, s. §§ 21. 25.

§ 5. In a few cases =a= is long [as in E. father]. (Comp. Holtzmann,
Altd. Gr., I, 3 et seq.).

(a) In foren words: =Silbânus= (_Silvanus_), =aurâli= (_orale_),
=spaíkulâtur= (_speculator_), =Peilâtus=, etc.;

(b) In the following Gothic words: =fâhan= (OHG. fâhan), _to cach_;
=hâhan= (OHG. hâhan), _to hang_; =þâhta= (prt. of =þagkjan=, _to
think_); =brâhta= (prt. of =briggan=, _to bring_); =gafâhs=, _a haul_;
=faúrhâh=, _curtain_; =gahâhjô=, _in order_; =-gâhts=, _a going_; also
=þâhô= (OHG. dâha), _clay_; =unwâhs=, _blameless_ (OE. wôh, _wrong_).

  NOTE. In the words mentiond under (b) =âh= arose from =anh= (§ 50,
  n. 1). Cp. also Litbl. 1886, p. 485.


e

§ 6. =e= is always a long, close vowel (=ê=) approaching very much the
sound of =i= [as in E. they].

  NOTE 1. In Greek words η is regularly represented by =ê=; e.
  g., =Gabriêl=, =Kêfas=, =aíkklêsjô=, =Krêta=; --sumtimes also
  ι: =Naên=, Ναίν; =Tykêkus=, Τυχικός; =aíloê=, ἐλωί; likewise e:
  =Jarêd=, Ἰαρέδ.

  NOTE 2. In Gothic names Latin writers employ =e= for Gothic =ê=:
  =Sigismêres=, =Gelimêr=, =Reccarêd=; besides, as erly as the 6th
  century, quite regularly also =i=; as, =Theodemir=, =Valamir=. Cp.
  Beitr., 11, 7 et seq.; Wrede, Wand., 92 et seq. #/Ναίν

§ 7. Goth. =ê= (which regularly corresponds to OHG. and OS. â; ahd.
gr., § 34) is found:

(a) in reduplicating verbs, in part with the ablaut =ô= (§§ 179.
181): =grêtan=, =lêtan=, =slêpan=; (b) in the prt. pl. of the IV.
and V. ablaut-series: =sêtum= (inf. =sitan=, _to sit_), =nêmun= (inf.
=niman=, _to take_), =têmum= (inf. =timan=, _to befit_), =êtum= (inf.
_itan_), and in the prt. sg. =frêt=; Luc. XV, 30 (§ 176, n. 3); (c)
in derivativs from the verbal stems givn under (b); as, =andanêms=,
_agreeabl_; =andanêm=, _a receiving_; =gatêmiba=, _becumingly_;
=uzêta=, _manger_; (d) in other words; as, =jêr=, _year_; =qêns=,
_wife_; =mêna=, _moon_; =lêkeis=, _fysician_; =mêrjan=, _to preach_;
=manasêþs= ('_man-seed_'), _world_, etc.; (e) in formativ syllabls:
=fahêþs=, _joy_; =awêþi=, _flock of sheep_ (cp. however § 17, n. 1);
=azêts=, _easy_; 2nd pers. sg. prt. of wvs., =-dês= (=nasidês=, § 184);
(f) final: in the ending of the gen. pl.; as, =dagê=; in monosyllabic
instrumentals: =þê=, =ƕê= (§§ 153. 159); in particls and advs.; as,
=swê=, =untê=, =hidrê=, =bisunjanê=; lastly, in the dativs =ƕammêh=,
=ƕarjammêh=, =ainummê-hun= (cp. §§ 163-166).

  NOTE 1. =ê= before vowels appears as =ai=; s. § 22.

  NOTE 2. =ei= occurs quite often for =ê=, especially in the Gospel
  of St. Luke; as, =qeins= (= =qêns=), =faheid= (= =fahêd=),
  =fraleitais= (= =fralêtais=); Lu. II, 5. 10. 29; =afleitan=; Mt.
  IX, 6, etc.

  NOTE 3. Sporadically also =i= for =ê=; so, frequently, in the
  Gospel of St. Lu.; as, =b~i~rusjôs=; Lu. II, 41; =q~i~þeina=; VIII,
  56. IX, 21; =tawid~i~deina=; VI, 11; =duatsn~i~wun=; Mk. VI, 53.
  Only =i= is found in =wriþus=, _herd_; Lu. VIII, 33 (for =wrêþus=;
  cp. Bezzenb. Beitr. 3, 114).

  NOTE 4. Reversely, also =e= occurs for =i= and =ei= (§ 10, n. 5; §
  17, n. 1).--These deviations (in ns. 2-4) seem due to East Gothic
  writers; cp. Wrede, 'Ostg.', 161.

§ 8. From the preceding =ê= must be separated the =ê= of sum Gothic
words in which it corresponds to OHG. ea, ia (not â): =hêr=, _here_;
=Krêks=, _Greek_; =fêra=, _side_, _region_; =mês=, _table_. Cp. ahd.
gr., §§ 35. 36; Beitr., 18, 409 et seq.


i

§ 9. Gothic =i=, as a rule, denotes the short vowel =i= [as in E. it],
while its corresponding long sound is represented by =ei= [= ie in E.
believ]; s. § 16.

  NOTE 1. The =i= in Greek words stands for short ι, only
  exceptionally for η which is generally represented by =ê=; e. g.,
  =Aúnisimus=, Ὀνήσιμος; =Biþania=, Βηθανία.

  NOTE 2. =i= in Gothic words is long, when it is incorrectly employd
  for =ê= (cp. § 7, n. 3).

§ 10. The Gothic =i=, from an historical point of view, is of two
kinds: It represents two originally distinct sounds which, from a
purely Gothic standpoint, can not be separated.

(a) Goth. =i= = proethnic Germanic e (OHG. ë or i; cp. ahd. gr., §§
28-30), as in the prs. tense of verbs of the III.-V. ablaut-series
(§§ 32-34): =niman=, OHG. nëman; =giban=, OHG. gëban; =giba=, OHG.
gëba; =bindan=, OHG. bintan; =itan=, _to eat_; =midjis=, '_medius_';
=hlifan=, _to steal_; =swistar=, OHG. swëster; =fidwôr=, _four_;
=gifts=, _gift_; =-qiss=, _speech_; the pps. of the V. ablaut-series:
=gibans=, =itans=, =lisans=, =wigans=, =qiþans=.

(b) Goth. =i= = proethnic Germanic i (OHG. i; ahd. gr., § 31); e. g.,
=lists=, _stratagem_; =fisks=, _fish_; =is=, _he_; =wissa=, _I knew_;
=skritnan=, _to rend_ (intr.); prt. pl. and pp. of the verbs of the
I. ablaut-series (§ 30): =bitun=, =bitans= (inf. =beitan=); =stigun=,
=stigans= (inf. =steigan=); =liþun=, =liþans= (inf. =leiþan=).

  NOTE 1. Final =i= occurs in =ni=, =bi=, =si=, =hiri=; in the
  nominativs of feminin and neuter =j=-stems: =bandi= (§ 96), =kuni=
  (§ 93); in the acc. and voc. sg. of the masculin =j=-stems: =hari=
  (§ 90); 3d pers. sg. prt. opt.: =nêmi=. This final =i= appears as
  =j=, when it becums medial (§ 45).

  NOTE 2. Final =i= before a following =i= of an enclitic word
  is elided in =nist= (= =ni-ist=), =sei= (= =si-ei=), =niba= (=
  =ni-iba=).

  NOTE 3. Every =i= before =h= and =r= is broken to =aí=; cp. § 20.

  NOTE 4. =ij= is found in =ija=, '_eam_'; =þrija=, '_tria_';
  =fijan=, _to hate_; =frijôn=, _to luv_; =sijum=, _we ar_; =kijans=,
  _germinated_, etc. =i= for =ij= is rare: =fian=, =sium=, etc., but
  =friaþwa= (beside =frijaþwa=), _luv_, occurs very often.

  NOTE 5. Occasionally =e= takes the place of =i=; as, =usdrebi=; Mk.
  V, 10; =seneigana=; I. Tim. V, 1.

  NOTE 6. For =i= in the difthong =iu=, s. §§ 18. 19.

  NOTE 7. For a separation of the two =i=s (= OHG. ë and i) in East
  Gothic names, s. Wrede, 'Ostg.', 162.


o

§ 11. The Gothic character =o= always denotes a long close =o=
approaching sumwhat the sound of =û= (= o in E. home).

  NOTE 1. In Greek words =o=, as a rule, corresponds to ω, rarely to
  ο; e. g., =Makidonja=, Μακεδονία; it also stands for ου: =Iodas=,
  Ἰούδας; Lu. III, 26.

  NOTE 2. =o= in Gothic words often stands for (short) =u= (§ 14, n.
  3).

§ 12. =ô= (= OHG. uo; s. ahd. gr., § 38 et seq.) is frequent in Gothic
words. E. g., =brôþar=, _brother_; =bôka=, _beech_; =frôþs=, _wise_;
=flôdus=, _flud_; =fôtus=, _foot_.

In the prt. of the VI. series (§ 35) and of the =ê--ô=-series (§ 36):
=ôl=, =hôf=, =ôg=, pl. =ôlum=, =hôfum=, =ôgum=;

> I, Maro Aurelian, lately honored by appointment from His Majesty’s own discerning hand to the post of Sub-Prefect of the *Decani Turres* of the Western Quadrant, hereby submit my first observations upon this noble institution, humbly conscious that no words may equal the brilliance of the royal design.

> **General Appraisal.**  The ten-tower system is a wonder of reason and foresight.  Each tower, though modest in girth, stands as a miniature kingdom: garrison, granary, and church in one.  The signal fires leap like obedient thoughts along the mountains, conveying His Majesty’s will swifter than rumor itself.  Truly, the towers are the vertebrae of Empire.  
>   
> **Condition of Works.**  I have inspected four thus far.  The masonry, while occasionally weathered, bears the royal monogram still sharp.  The staircases creak, yet the spirit of the men does not.  In several posts the fire-pits have sunk; the local captains assure me they will rise again when ordered.  I have expressed my deepest confidence in their zeal and reminded them that neglect of a royal flame is treason to light itself.  They appeared suitably moved.  
>   
> **Personnel.**  The watchmen are of mixed stock—Gothic veterans, Moravian recruits, and one Lusatian whose manners are rustic but whose eyesight borders on prophecy.  I have begun addressing them as *sons of the King’s flame*; they cheer at this and salute twice.  I record this success for possible inclusion in the official catechism of service.  
>   
> **Discipline and Morale.**  In every tower I recited the royal oath aloud before dawn, adding extemporaneous praise to His Majesty’s courage in establishing such a glorious chain.  The men joined enthusiastically, though one fainted from smoke inhalation.  I regard this as a good omen of devotion.  
>   
> **Communication Efficiency.**  On the night of the 14th inst., I ordered a trial illumination across three ridges.  The first fire was lit at the tenth hour; the third answered within the half of a psalm.  The spectacle drew villagers from ten leagues, who declared that the heavens themselves seemed to write the King’s name in flame.  I have suggested to the Treasury that a commemorative medal be struck, perhaps bearing my initials in small relief.  
>   
> **Security Concerns.**  There are rumors from the northern marches—ships, smoke, and stories that travel faster than fact.  I have counseled all tower-masters to maintain vigilance and to dedicate each night’s flame to the royal peace.  Should the enemy approach, he will find the kingdom already lit against him.  
>   
> **Recommendations.**  More oil, less poetry from the garrison priests, and permission for me to design a uniform plume distinctive to my office (to enhance morale).  I remain utterly convinced that His Majesty’s vision of a luminous frontier shall endure as long as mountains exist to hold torches.  
>   
> Written in trembling gratitude beneath the banner of the Crown,  
>   
> **Sub-Prefect Maro Aurelian of Latium,**  
> Servant of the Light and of the Most Radiant King.”

>

>

#### **“The Thirty-First Night,” by CAPTAIN GAREMUND SON OF OSRIC**  
*Written on scraped vellum, smoke-stained and salt-stiff; found rolled inside a broken signal-horn.  No royal countersign appears, only the scratch of a soldier’s hand.*

> “To any officer of the Crown who still holds a tower,  
>   
> I, Garemund son of Osric, captain of the northern watch, send what may be my last account.  The Sub-Prefect Maro Aurelian is alive, more or less—kept by the raiders for ransom or sport.  They hang his plume from the palisade to remind us what enthusiasm costs.  
>   
> **Situation.**  Hvozd is encircled.  The sea brought them—thirty ships, long and narrow, painted white with lime and blood.  They row even through storm.  Their leader wears a wolf’s skull over mail; his men whistle when they loose arrows, as if calling dogs.  
>   
> Our outer walls fell on the fifth day; the inner keep holds.  The wells are brackish, the pitch nearly gone.  We burn fish-oil now, and the smoke stinks of penance.  When the wind turns, the enemy laughs—the sound carries like children at play.  
>   
> **Losses.**  Two towers silenced, one taken and lit against us.  Sergeant Hrodgar threw himself into the firepit rather than yield.  I marked his name in the margin of the muster roll; the ink bled outward, as men do.  
>   
> **Morale.**  The younger soldiers still believe relief will come.  The older ones—like me—keep watch because it is what we have always done.  When the bells of Budzina fail to answer, we pretend they are still ringing under the wind.  
>   
> **On Faith.**  The priests argue Arius against Athanasius between volleys.  I tell them God will take whichever side still has arrows.  Yet when the dawn breaks red, even I feel the old creed: *The Son is lesser, but the lesser suffers first.*  Perhaps that is why we fight.  
>   
> **Orders Executed.**  The beacon was lit last night though half the men wanted to save the oil.  I told them a king’s eyes need proof we are not yet ghosts.  The fire caught quick, ran up the mast, and for one breath the sky remembered us.  If Albensis saw, then the realm still breathes.  
>   
> **Personal.**  I served in four campaigns before this one, all of them forgotten.  I have no wife, no sons, only scars that whistle in rain.  If this letter reaches any officer of rank, tell them the towers held as promised.  Tell them the Sub-Prefect kept smiling even when they broke his fingers.  Tell them the north is burning, but in pattern—each blaze where a beacon should be.  
>   
> **Recommendation.**  Do not ransom Maro Aurelian; he would only write again.  Send ships instead, or send the King himself if courage is still part of ceremony.  
>   
> The enemy drums at sunset.  I will answer with iron at dawn.  This is the thirty-first night.  The smoke leans inland, toward the heartland.  Tell them it is not a plea for aid, but a message of duty: the light still burns.  
>   
> *Garemund son of Osric,*  
> *Captain of the Tower at Hvozd.*”  

---

#### **Modern Biographic Note:**  
**Captain Garemund Osricsson (c. 705 – 780 P.C.)** — A career frontier officer from the western marches, transferred north during the early phase of the *Serpent War*. The letter’s blend of bitterness, gallows humor, and stoic devotion became canonical in later Bogothic military literature.  Modern analysts believe his final beacon signal marked the turning point of the Northern Alarm: a communication chain built for ceremony used, at last, for salvation.

#### **I. To the Praefect of the Northern Roads — the 3rd Night**  
> “My lord,  
>   
> The wind here smells of pitch and brine.  Our beacon smokes more than it shines; still, we light it each dusk.  The Sub-Prefect, bless his gilded tongue, insists the flame must ‘proclaim the King’s glory.’  I told him it would be easier to proclaim it if the oil reached us on time.  
>   
> I remind the Crown that my blood is of **Osric the Younger**, who rode in the last cohort out of Ravenna and built the first watchtower at the Morava ford.  He wrote that the world ends where men stop keeping watch.  I have not stopped.  
>   
> Send powder.  Send prayers that do not rhyme.”  

---

#### **II. To the Royal Quartermaster at Velehrad — the 6th Night**  
> “Your manifests lie.  They say we have salt meat for ten days; we have mold for two.  We boil horsehide, and it smells of sermons.  The men eat while pretending it is beef, and faith keeps them from vomiting.  
>   
> My grandsire fought at Blatna, knee-deep in mud and arrows.  He said the difference between Rome and barbarism was who kept the books.  I keep mine still—see attached list of the dead.  I write each name slow, so the ink dries before the next.  There is time.  There is always too much time.  
>   
> Tell the mints of Albensis that when the siege is done, I will pay the treasury in enemy skulls.”  

---

#### **III. To His Excellency the Chancellor — the 10th Night**  
> “I have read the court’s message urging ‘restraint and composure.’  Come show us how.  
>   
> The enemy drums without rhythm, just noise.  They whistle as they kill, and it makes the night seem longer.  
>   
> They have taken Maro Aurelian.  He still talks, even from their palisade, though I think his words are for himself now.  They wave his feathered hat on a pike and shout ‘Peace!’ each time our archers aim.  The irony is not lost.  
>   
> When my father died, he said, ‘We carried the Empire on our backs, and it broke us straight.’  I think of him when the tower groans under the wind.”  

---

#### **IV. To the Bishop of Olomucia — the 16th Night**  
> “You wrote last winter asking if the garrison would accept the Latin creed.  I write now from a tower ringed with corpses and tell you this: we pray to whatever listens.  My men kneel to the Arian God, the Athanasian God, and one old Slav carves the names of his cattle for luck.  All of them fight as brothers.  
>   
> My ancestor **Osric the Elder** fell on the steps of Ravenna’s basilica holding a banner too heavy for one man.  He said the same thing before he died: *‘All faiths are tested by fire.’*  Consider us well examined.”  

---

#### **V. To Any Officer South of the River — the 23rd Night**  
> “We can see their watchfires from the tower top—fifty at least.  The sky looks like an anvil.  
>   
> The men joke that we are now the ‘Last Legion of Ravenna.’  They are wrong.  We are not legion; we are ten dozen tired men and a half-burnt Sub-Prefect’s hat.  But I understand the comfort of names.  The ghosts of my line would approve.  
>   
> When I was a boy, my mother said Osric’s descendants were marked by smoke; wherever we go, something burns.  She was right.  Tonight the north wind carries the smell of home.”

#### **VI. To the Royal Chancellery — the 28th Night**  
> “If you receive this, it means a runner broke the line.  He carries three copies—one for record, one for rumor, one for memory.  Use whichever survives.  
>   
> Hvozd still holds.  The gate is splintered, but the walls stand.  The men are down to half rations and double courage.  We have melted the Sub-Prefect’s ornamental plate for arrowheads; he would have approved, if conscious.  
>   
> When the first Amaleric fled Ravenna, my ancestors swore that our exile would not be a retreat but a redirection.  I think we are reaching the end of that road.  If we fall, let it be forward.”

#### **VII. To His Majesty Amaleric II — the 31st Night**  
> “Sire,  
>   
> I have no couriers left.  This letter will travel by sea, if the sea still remembers loyalty.  
>   
> The enemy is through the outer yard.  We have doused the beacon, for the flame drew their arrows.  I light this letter with a coal from it instead.  My hand shakes more from cold than fear.  
>   
> I have stood my watch as my fathers did—at Ravenna, at Blatna, at the Morava.  They all ended the same way: surrounded, outnumbered, unforgotten.  There is dignity in repetition.  
>   
> Tell the realm the towers burned in order, not in panic.  Tell them we kept the line until the end.  And tell them that when the fire reached me, I saluted.  
>   
> *Garemund Osricsson,*  
> *Captain of the Tower at Hvozd*.”

### **The Chronicle of the Late Watchman**  
*(Commonly called *The Villa Letters* or *The Silver Chronicle*; written by Garemund Osricsson in the final decade of his life, after the Serpent War, at his villa near Kutná Hora.  Surviving manuscripts held in the Albensian Academy, copied from his own smoke-stained folios.)*

#### **Prefatory Note (dictated to his scribe, Mlada of Zbraslav)**  

> “They made me an historian because I refused to die on time.  
> The king took my sword, gave me paper, and said, *‘Write what you saw, that our sons may not learn courage by accident.’*  
> I obey, though I have learned that memory cuts deeper than steel.  
>   
> The villa lies on a hillside above Kutná Hora, where the earth bleeds silver.  I hear the miners at dusk and think the ground itself is coughing up its ghosts.  It is a fitting place for a man who has already buried his noise.”

---

### **I. Of the War’s Ending**

> “After the *Northern Correction* there was no victory—only distance between fires.  The sea left us its dead, the king left us his silence.  
> The raiders vanished, taking the Sub-Prefect’s bones and our appetite for glory.  
> The realm called it peace; we veterans called it the pause.  
>   
> I rode south with the king’s cortege as far as Moravia, saw him cough blood into a silver cup, and knew the old line of Amaleric was ending as it had begun—in exile disguised as pilgrimage.  He spoke little.  Only once did he say, *‘We have carried Ravenna far enough; let the next century find its own walls.’*  
> I bowed.  What else can a soldier do when history itself grows tired?”  

---

### **II. Of the Realm in Aftermath**

> “The capital smelled of incense and paperwork.  The clerks wrote the war into triumph, gilding each failure until it shone.  The towers were rebuilt, yes—but thinner, less sure of their purpose.  
> The younger officers drilled with more polish than faith.  The priests argued whether the northern dead were martyrs or simply poor logisticians.  
>   
> I retired before they decided.  A veteran must know when he has become someone else’s metaphor.”  

---

### **III. Of the Villa and Its Inhabitants**

> “My estate lies among fields that once belonged to men I never met.  The peasants call me *Starý Vlčák*—the Old Wolf—and bring me milk and questions.  I teach their children to write their names and to count to ten using arrowheads as tokens.  
>   
> Each morning I walk the vineyard slope.  The vines grow stubborn here, gripping the same stones that tore my boots during the campaigns.  I have begun to think the land remembers us better than our own kings do.  
>   
> The miners dig silver day and night.  I visit their shafts sometimes.  The air smells of coin and sweat.  They carve prayers into the beams—Arian, Latin, pagan—anything that might hold the roof.  When one of them dies, I copy his name into my ledger of the fallen.  It is an old habit.”  

---

### **IV. Of Faith**

> “I remain Arian, though the bishops call us ‘the cooled fire.’  Perhaps they are right.  My God is still the First-Made, a soldier promoted to divinity.  I find comfort in that hierarchy.  
> The priests of Kutná Hora preach that Heaven is a city of light.  I prefer to think it a watchtower—manned, vigilant, unadorned.  If the Son is indeed lesser than the Father, then He stands the longer watch.  
>   
> When I pray, I do not kneel.  I stand, as we did on the walls of Hvozd, eyes open to the wind.”  

---

### **V. Of History and Forgetting**

> “The chroniclers of Albensis sent me their drafts of the war.  In them, I am already dead.  They have me falling beside the beacon, a tidy ending.  I wrote back: *‘I am still here, and the beacon still smokes.’*  They replied with silence, the historian’s form of correction.  
>   
> So I write my own account, though I suspect no one will read it until I am safely myth again.  Let it be known that wars are not won by kings or sermons but by men who remember the road home.  
>   
> My ancestors fled Ravenna with nothing but a banner and a list of names.  I keep both still.  The banner hangs above my hearth, faded to the color of bone; the list grows longer each winter.”  

---

### **VI. Of the Next Generation**

### **Excerpt from *Historiensis: Or the Record of Civilitas Restored***  
*(Written in the final years of Garemund Osricsson’s life at Kutná Hora, circa 785–790 P.C.; compiled posthumously by his scribe Mlada and partially redacted by later royal editors.  The following passage is from Book IV, “On Kings and the Weight of Their Mirrors.”)*  

---

> “History, to those who live off it, is a kind of pasture—soft grass for the courtiers who fatten on praise, and dung for the rest of us to wade through.  I have seen too many scribes call a famine ‘a prudent redistribution,’ and too many kings believe it.  I write not for comfort but for proportion.  
>   
> The kingdom, when measured truly, is not a ladder reaching heavenward but a wheel—its spokes are rivers, its rim is rumor, and its hub is law.  Turn it too long without greasing it with truth and it shrieks.  My task has been to listen to that noise and call it music.  
>   
> The syncophants—those pleasant birds in the royal rafters—say that Amaleric’s victories were divine.  I say they were logistical.  They call his decrees eternal; I call them legible, which is better.  They will never forgive me for it.  The flatterer sells perfume; I sell weather reports.  Both fill the air, but only one helps you plan a march.  
>   
> In my youth I thought kings needed poets.  In my age I know they need mirrors.  Not the polished kind that return a handsome lie, but the warped bronze that shows the dents in a crown.  My duty was to hold that mirror steady, though the hand shook.  
>   
> The realm I see from this villa’s hill is vast and various—  
> The western mines hum like organs; men pray to profit and call it providence.  
> The Moravian plain is green with grain and argument.  
> The northern marches still dream of the sea that nearly devoured them.  
> In Albensis the scribes polish their vowels until meaning slides off.  
> Yet through all of it runs one cord: the habit of endurance.  The Bogothic state survives not because it is loved, nor feared, nor even understood, but because it is too accustomed to continuing to do otherwise.  
>   
> Let later historians dress these truths in velvet.  I have written them in homespun.  The king himself once told me, *‘Garemund, your pen makes enemies of all my friends.’*  I replied, *‘Majesty, then my pen has done what your sword could not.’*  He laughed; the courtiers did not.  He was a good king for that reason alone.  
>   
> When the towers burn again—and they will, for it is the nature of towers to burn—may there be someone left willing to describe the smoke honestly.  Let the next historian remember that the wind, not the herald, decides which way history blows.  
>   
> I have tried to keep my prose clear enough that a farmer may understand and a minister may sweat.  That, I am told, is unpardonable.”

### **Contextual Commentary (Albensian Academy Edition, 15th century)**  

Scholars note that *Historiensis* scandalized the court historians of its day for its candor and its unmistakable drift toward Procopian irony—celebrating the glories of the realm while dissecting their absurdities.  Osricsson’s “wheel of law” metaphor was interpreted as an implicit rebuke of the Divine Hierarchy; his description of kings as “men who borrow tomorrow’s loyalty to pay today’s applause” was struck from later editions.  

Yet kings themselves treasured his work in private.  Amaleric II kept a copy in his field tent during the Northern Campaign; later monarchs annotated the margins with nervous agreement.  To the bureaucrats, Osricsson was dangerous.  To rulers who feared oblivion more than criticism, he was indispensable: the one chronicler who could be trusted to tell the truth and make it survive.  

Thus, the very honesty that exiled him from polite scholarship became his immortality.  In later centuries his name turned proverb:  
**“Write as Osricsson saw—clear, and at peril.”**

> “The priests have often told me that a man must choose between the sword and the sermon.  
> They are wrong.  I have held both, and neither drew less blood.  
>   
> In the year when the famine met the king’s pride at the same table, the Council of Albensis declared that the Nicene creed should be our law of Heaven. >   
> They summoned us soldiers to the basilica, bade us kneel, and taught us the new words.  *“Of one substance with the Father,”* we repeated, though half the men thought it a ration decree.  I said the words aloud and tasted nothing.  My mouth knew discipline better than doctrine.  
>   
> For a season it held.  The banners bore the Latin cross; the bishops’ rings gleamed brighter than their eyes.  Even the king, weary of division, bent his head to the imported creed.  He meant peace, and I will not mock him for that.  
>   
> But peace written on parchment is lighter than wind.  The peasants kept their old hymns, the monks kept their old doubts, and the veterans still prayed as they had on the walls of Hvozd: to the Son who fights, not the Father who observes.  
>

>   
> I do not know which is truer, and I care less each year.  I have seen brave men of both creeds die with equal clarity in their eyes.  If Heaven exists, it will sort its theology without my help.  
>   
> What I know is this: when the Nicenes ruled our tongues, the realm went silent; when the Arians sang again, the forges rang in time with the psalms.  There is more faith in a hammer than in a quarrel over essence.  
>   
> The scholars call us heretics.  They are welcome to their word.  We never claimed to be saints; we claimed to be survivors.  The Son, they say, is ‘begotten not made.’  I saw sons made every day in war: by fear, by hunger, by command.  If He learned obedience through suffering, then He is one of us.  
>   
> The Church, being clever, decided to bless our defiance retroactively.  They call it a ‘local variation.’  I call it honesty.  The Nicene decree remains in the books, like an old oath no one remembers how to pronounce.  But the people still raise their children to believe what they can touch, what bleeds, what answers.  
>   
> And so the Arian flame endures—not in councils, but in cellars; not in marble, but in muscle.  It has the stubbornness of stone and the warmth of smoke.  It asks nothing but endurance, and that we have always had.  
>   
> I write these things not as believer or blasphemer, but as witness.  I have seen kingdoms die of too much holiness.  Better a faith that sweats than one that preaches.  Let the bishops debate; the plowman will still look skyward and whisper thanks to whichever god spares his crop.  That, I think, is religion enough for any realm.  
>   
> When I die, I wish no priest to bless me.  Let a soldier close my eyes and a scribe record the hour.  If Heaven wants me, it will find me standing guard.”

Osricsson’s *De Fide et Fervore* was considered incendiary in its time—not for rejecting Nicene orthodoxy, which many still privately doubted, but for treating belief as a social instrument rather than revelation. The archivists never reconciled them—perhaps because, in the long light of the realm’s history, the two had become the same.

This passage shows the young Garemund at his most ceremonious: full of balance, imagery, and the moral geometry typical of early Bogothic historiography.  It is the language of a loyal captain writing for kings, not yet the wounded philosopher of Kutná Hora.

### **Modern Commentary**

Theodric’s *Gothorum Gentis Origines* became the canonical “ethnography of conversion” for the late Arian monarchy.  Its rolling prose and gentle irony mark it as the mature Bogothic counterpart to Bede: a theologian writing history as cultural reconciliation.

### **Mlada of Zbraslav (later known as *Sister Mlada Scriptoria*)**  
*(c. 745 – 812 P.C., fl. 770–805 P.C.)*  

---

#### **I.  Summary of Life and Work**

Mlada of Zbraslav is now recognized as one of the foundational figures of Bogothic letters—a scribe, grammarian, and cultural mediator whose innovations in script and syntax helped fuse the Gothic and Slavic traditions into a single written continuum.  For centuries she was treated as a footnote to the chronicles of Garemund Osricsson; modern philological study has restored her as his equal partner and, in many ways, his successor.

---

#### **II.  Origins and Education**

Born to a family of minor foresters near the Moravian border town of Zbraslav, Mlada came of age in a period of both religious and linguistic turbulence: the late Arian revival in the north and the first Glagolitic missions pushing upward from the south.  
Local records—partly reconstructed from tithe rolls—suggest she was literate in both the Gothic Koine and the evolving southern Slav vernacular by adolescence, a rarity for women of her station.  A travelling clerk of the Albensian chancery is thought to have trained her in the *Ulfila* script; the Glagolitic she learned from missionaries fleeing famine near Mikulov.

---

#### **III.  Association with Garemund Osricsson**

By the late 770s she appears in court rosters as *Mlada scriptrix veterana* in the northern military archive.  During the post-war years she entered the household of Captain (later historian) Garemund Osricsson at Kutná Hora.  Whether as secretary, collaborator, or confidante, she served as the physical hand of much of his later work—including *Historiensis* and *De Fide et Fervore*.  
Their partnership, later twisted by propagandists into gossip and heresy, was above all a collaboration between two forms of literacy: his martial, declarative prose and her supple, comparative linguistics.

---

#### **IV.  The *Reform of the Hand***  

Between 780 and 790 P.C. Mlada composed a series of teaching tables known collectively as *Tabula Mladana*, in which she experimented with hybridizing the angular Gothic Ulfila and the ornate Glagolitic scripts.  The resulting *Liutisk Majuscula* introduced:

1. **Soft vowel markers** derived from Glagolitic open rounds;  
2. **Binding strokes** allowing ligature between alphabets;  
3. **Dual-duty consonants**, serving phonetic needs of both north and south.  

Her grammar notes also systematized the *Koine* as a truly written language rather than a spoken military jargon, providing a literary backbone for the late Bogothic renaissance.

---

#### **V.  Faith and Philosophy**

Nominally Arian, Mlada’s writings display what modern scholars call *scriptural pragmatism*: she viewed faith through its languages.  Her surviving marginalia record no prayers, only observations such as “*The creed that cannot be copied cannot be believed*.”  She regarded transcription as a moral act—each faithful copy an argument against decay.

---

#### **VI.  Later Years and Legacy**

After Garemund’s death (c. 792 P.C.) she remained at the Villa Silva for two winters, editing and organizing his papers before taking vows at the Abbey of Saint Radegund.  There she continued teaching until her death, recorded laconically in the abbey annals: *“Sister Mlada Scriptoria, who wrote as well as she prayed, entered the Light.”*

Her influence outlived her name.  Every Bogothic charter from the 9th century onward bears traces of her hand—the rounded vowels, the understated ligatures, the rhythm between command and song.  By the 13th century she was half-legend, patroness of scribes, invoked with the saying:  
**“Ink remembers better than stone.”**

---

#### **VII.  Modern Assessment**

Cross-disciplinary research from the Albensian Academy and the Moravian Epigraphic Project (1980s–2020s editions of the *Corpus Liutiskum*) confirms that at least three of the oldest mixed-script documents in existence—the *Kutná Hora Charter*, the *Moravian Baptistery Inscription*, and fragments of the *Codex Ravennavensis*—were penned in her hand or that of her immediate students.  

Historians now regard Mlada as:

- **The first identifiable female grammarian** of the Central European continuum;  
- **Architect of the Liutisk writing system**, precursor to both later Slavic and Western runiform scripts;  
- **Bridge figure** between the Arian revival and the later humanist secularism of the early second millennium.  

In the words of modern philologist Dana Karlsdotter (2021):  

> “Mlada did not merely copy Bogothia’s history—she rewrote the nervous system through which it remembered itself.”
